verses.1: Al-Mizan links this opening glorification with the sūrah's final verse. Its mention of Allah's might and wisdom suits the ensuing account of Jewish betrayal and covenant-breaking, the hypocrites' deceitful assurances, and the divinely wise consequences they were made to taste.
verses.2: Al-Mizan explains ḥashr as an upheaval-filled banishment and li-awwal al-ḥashr as the initial expulsion of Banū al-Naḍīr from the Arabian Peninsula. Their apparent strength and many fortresses made their departure unexpected, but their strongholds could not defend against Allah. He reached them through what they did not expect—their hearts—by casting terror into them. They destroyed their own houses to prevent seizure, while believers destroyed what Allah commanded them to destroy; this is the apparent explanation, though escape and symbolic social collapse are reported alternatives. Their covenant-breaking led to this outcome, which is a lesson in Allah's response to opposition to Him and His Messenger.
verses.3: Al-Mizan says the decreed banishment was itself Allah's worldly judgment on them. Had He not ordained their departure from homeland and homes, they would have received worldly punishment—expulsion, killing, or captivity, like Banū Qurayẓa—while the punishment of the Fire remains for them in the Hereafter.
verses.4: Al-Mizan glosses shāqqū as persistent defiance and grounds their expulsion and deserved punishment in opposition to Allah and His Messenger. Repeating opposition to Allah alone after naming both subtly establishes that opposing the Messenger is opposing Allah; His retribution is severe.
verses.5: Al-Mizan reports that, when the Prophet ordered palms felled, people objected that this was mischief on the earth. The verse answers that every al-līnah, a tender palm without restriction to one variety, was cut or left by Allah's will. The causal lām in ‘that He may disgrace the transgressors’ indicates among the purposes of that command the disgrace of Banū al-Naḍīr.
verses.6: Al-Mizan defines al-ifāʾah as the return of war spoils and identifies ‘from them’ as Banū al-Naḍīr's wealth. Because no horses or camels were spurred in combat—their fortresses were near Madinah and the approach was on foot—this fayʾ belonged to the Messenger's control and discretion. Allah nonetheless made His Messenger prevail over them and could authorize the wealth's distribution and use as He willed.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that fayʾ from towns is entrusted to the Messenger: ‘for Allah’ is a share spent in His way under the Messenger's judgment, not a merely blessing-seeking phrase, and the Messenger also has his own share. ‘Relatives’ means the Prophet's kin, not every believer's; the separate mention of orphans gives special attention to their destitute. Reports from the Imams of the Prophet's Household identify the relatives as that Household and the orphans, needy, and traveller as those among them. The distribution prevents wealth from circulating only among the affluent. In its immediate context, taking what the Messenger gives and relinquishing what he forbids requires acceptance of his allocation; apart from that context it encompasses every command and prohibition of the Messenger, and the warning against Allah reinforces it.

Al-Mizan considers several syntactical accounts of the poor Emigrants. It gives priority to treating them as an actual instance of spending in Allah's way, rather than as direct statutory shareholders: the Prophet distributes according to his judgment. Thus the reports that he gave Banū al-Naḍīr's fayʾ chiefly to Emigrants, with only the impoverished Anṣār Abū Dujānah Samak b. Kharshah, Sahl b. Ḥunayf, and al-Ḥārith b. al-Simmah receiving it, record discretionary spending in Allah's way. These pre-conquest Meccan migrants had been forced from homes and property; they seek provision as Allah's grace and His pleasure in the Hereafter, support Allah and His Messenger with property and lives, and are called truthful for that sincerity.

The commentary then praises the Anṣār, settled in the land and faith before the emigrants. It discusses whether this is a new commendation or a continuation of the allocation discourse, and whether the three recipients show their collective inclusion, while maintaining that the ultimate distribution lay with the Prophet's judgment. A translator's note says the intricate syntactical discussion is paraphrased for clarity. The Anṣār loved the migrants, felt neither need, constriction, nor envy over what they received, and preferred them despite their own poverty. Al-Mizan defines shuḥ as stinginess joined to intense habitual desire; those whom Allah protects from it, both in withholding what they possess and envying others' possessions, are the successful.

verses.10: Al-Mizan allows ‘those who came after them’ either to begin a new subject or to continue the preceding construction. It identifies them as later believers after the Muhājirūn and Anṣār, after migration ended with the conquest, or as their successors. Their prayer for themselves and their earlier brethren expresses solidarity: they seek forgiveness for all and ask that no ghill, deep-seated rancor, remain toward any believer, earlier or contemporary. The concluding appeal to Allah's kindness and mercy completes this love founded solely on faith.
verses.11: Al-Mizan treats the interrogative as astonishment at the hypocrites, identified as ʿAbdullāh b. Ubayy and his companions, who call Banū al-Naḍīr their brethren through shared affiliation. They emphatically promise to leave with them, refuse every contrary counsel, and aid them if fought. Allah's witness that they are liars directly declares that they will not keep any of these pledges.
verses.12: Al-Mizan calls this a detailed refutation of the hypocrites' promise. It repeats the emphatic oath that they will neither depart with Banū al-Naḍīr nor aid them in battle. Even the counterfactual possibility of their help would bring no lasting benefit: they would flee and then receive no help, left to destruction.
verses.13: Al-Mizan says the hypocrites' greater dread of believers than of Allah explains why they would not fight or stand with their allies. Their defect is lack of true understanding: had they understood that all good and harm, authority and power come only by Allah's permission and strength, they would fear Him alone.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan says neither Banū al-Naḍīr nor the hypocrites will meet believers in open battle, but only from fortified towns or behind walls. Their apparent collective might is ruthlessness toward one another; before believers, Allah-cast terror makes them cowardly. Though they look united, their hearts are disunited, a chief cause of defeat, because they do not reason.

The following likeness is directed specifically to Banū al-Naḍīr: like Banū Qaynuqāʿ, who recently broke their covenant after Badr, trusted hypocritical promises of intercession, were banished, and tasted their conduct's evil consequence, they face painful punishment. The alternative that it refers to Meccan disbelievers at Badr is less fitting to the context. The Satan-and-man likeness then depicts the hypocrites' false promise to Banū al-Naḍīr and betrayal when needed, just as Satan beautifies worldly pleasures, lures humans to disbelief with empty promise, and disavows them when the Hereafter's reality appears. A reported Barṣīṣā story may also be intended; another view connects the man to Abū Jahl at Badr and takes Satan's fear as earnest fear of the angels, whereas under the former readings his claim of fear is scorn and humiliation.

verses.17: Al-Mizan takes the dual pronouns as Satan and the human deceived by him: both remain in the Fire, the requital of wrongdoers. The same end applies to the hypocrites for deceptive promises and betrayal and to Banū al-Naḍīr for trusting them and persisting in defiance.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan reads the first command of taqwā as carrying out every obligation and avoiding every prohibition, then adds a distinct duty of self-accountability: each soul must inspect what it has sent ahead for the Resurrection, called ‘tomorrow’ for its nearness. If deeds are good, one may hope for reward; if corrupt, one must repent and return to Allah. This is like a craftsman’s second corrective review, and asks even whether apparently righteous works are accepted and pure. Although the address is universal, the indefinite ‘every soul’ gently rebukes the community and suggests how rare this reflective practice is amid worldly preoccupation.

The repeated taqwā is not merely reinforcement, repentance for past sins versus future avoidance, or duties versus prohibitions; Al-Mizan rejects those divisions. The first governs the initial performance of deeds, while the second follows self-examination to amend already performed deeds, preserve their sincerity, and protect them from corrupting factors, because Allah knows what people do. The adjoining warning against those who forget Allah reinforces this call to remembrance. Forgetting Him makes people forget their own souls: they imagine independent life, power, knowledge, and perfection, rely on themselves and apparent causes, and hope, fear, and seek tranquillity where only the Lord should be relied on, feared, hoped in, and sought. In reality, human beings are contingent, ignorant, powerless, humble, needy, and dependent, while every apparent perfection belongs ultimately to Allah. The warning is framed through the example of those who forgot Allah—such as Banū al-Naḍīr and Banū Qaynuqāʿ and those like them—because self-forgetfulness follows from that cause. Their transgression is departure from servitude; the paired verses make self-accountability and divine remembrance the required safeguards.

verses.20: Al-Mizan defines al-fawz as attaining good together with security. In context, the Fire's inmates are those who forget Allah and Paradise's inhabitants are those who remember Him. Humanity therefore divides into these two unequal groups with no third position, and everyone must join the remembering, God-conscious party whose outcome is success.
verses.21: Al-Mizan reports Majmaʿ al-bayān's gloss of al-taṣadduʿ as splitting after union, like shattering, and takes the verse as an imaginative similitude, not a literal event. The Qur'an's knowledge, fundamentals of divine law, moral instruction, exhortation, and warning are so majestic that a mountain, despite its hardness and endurance, would humble itself and break from fear of Allah were revelation capable of being sent upon it. Human beings should therefore be still more humbled when reciting or hearing it; the unyielding defiant heart is astonishing. The shift to ‘fear of Allah’ states the cause: it is His word. The general form of the closing comparisons extends the lesson beyond this case, inviting reflection, understanding, and obedience along the path of servitude, which the preceding discussion calls al-murāqabah and al-muḥāsabah.
verses.22: Al-Mizan says these verses enumerate Beautiful Names, directing those who remember Allah to invoke Him through them and know their own imperfection through His perfection. They also explain why the mountain would break in fear. ‘Allah—there is no god except Him’ declares the unique Divine Name, His sole divinity and worthiness of worship. The sensible or witnessed and the Unseen are relational: what one being perceives may be hidden from another according to its means of comprehension, but all are wholly known to Allah. Creatures know the unseen only when He discloses it, while His essence is absolutely unseen and beyond their comprehension, as (Al-Jinn: 26-27) and (20:110) indicate. The discussion of the All-beneficent and All-merciful is referred back to Sūrah Al-Fātiḥa.
verses.23: Al-Mizan glosses the listed Names: the Sovereign governs people's affairs; the All-holy is supremely transcendent and pure; the All-benign gives peace and safety; the Securer gives assurance; and the All-conserver exercises supreme dominion. The All-mighty cannot be overcome, the All-compeller repairs what is broken or enforces His will, and the All-magnanimous manifests greatness. The final declaration of His freedom from partners is exaltation of Allah, like the repudiation of the claim that He has taken a son in (2:116).
verses.24:
Al-Mizan distinguishes the Creator, who brings things into existence with measure, the Maker or Originator, who differentiates creations, and the Former, who gives their distinct forms; these aspects of creation have an inherent sequence. The eleven Names in the preceding verses are essential attributes of lordship and governance, independently true only of Allah, and so ground His exclusive divinity and worthiness of worship. By contrast, creation alone does not establish that exclusivity, since polytheists acknowledged Allah's creation while worshipping others.

The repetition of ‘He is Allah’ marks the Divine Essence as the confluence of all perfect attributes, while ‘to Him belong the Best Names’ includes every name beyond those enumerated. All created things in heavens and earth glorify Him. His ending as All-mighty and All-wise means that no disobedience frustrates His legislation and guidance and no faithful obedience goes unrewarded; it also underlines that the Qur'an itself is the speech of the Mighty, Wise God, and is characterized by might and wisdom.
